Pre-Socratic inquiry asks what nature is and how things come to be. In the Phaedo (96a–99d), Plato’s Socrates recalls his own early interest in such explanations and his disappointment with accounts that leave out why something is best.
Apollo’s oracle at Delphi: Chaerephon asks whether anyone is wiser than Socrates. The answer is no (Apology 20e–21a). The Delphic maxim “know yourself” is a different saying; Socrates invokes it in the Phaedrus (229e–230a).
Wisdom
Lecture summary:

Begins in self-understanding

What is the way we ought to live?
Socrates tests the oracle by questioning people reputed to be wise. His advantage is limited: when he lacks knowledge, he does not assume he has it (Apology 21b–23b). The craftsmen know their crafts; their mistake is taking that expertise as authority about everything important.
Philo-sophia: love of wisdom. In Diotima’s account in the Symposium (203e–204b), the philosopher recognises a lack and seeks wisdom. The already-wise have no need to seek it; the complacently ignorant see no need. Her account places Eros, a daimon, between mortal and divine (202d–203a).
Socrates asks: what is $X$?

What account applies to every case?
What explains why a particular thing is an instance of $X$?

In the Euthyphro (6d–8b), calling pious whatever the gods love produces a problem when the gods disagree: the same act could count as both pious and impious. The definition has to survive that contradiction.

Platonic Idea (Form)
The idea of X is the form all particular Xs share, and which cause them to be X.

This lecture summary matches the explanatory role Plato gives Forms in the Phaedo (100b–101d): beautiful things are beautiful through Beauty. A Form is intelligible and stable; a particular body can change. These are claims made through Socrates in Plato’s dialogues, so they need to be distinguished from a secure account of the historical Socrates.
Charges for Athenian trials?
Animosity with regards to his way of being?
Sources: Plato, Apology, Phaedo, Phaedrus, Symposium, and Euthyphro, at the passages above.
